name: Podcast Sponsorship Media Kit
description: An editorial sponsorship media kit for turning a podcast's positioning, audience evidence, content fit, host-read inventory, package pricing, and reporting commitments into a clear sales proposal.
style_guide:
# Podcast Sponsorship Media Kit

## Design intent

Create a credible, buyer-friendly media kit for an independent podcast, podcast network, or branded audio property. The visual language balances editorial warmth and measurable media: cream paper, near-black evidence panels, deep teal brand signals, coral editorial emphasis, bold sans-serif headlines, restrained italics, studio photography, and modular rate-card structures.

The deck should show what the program is, who listens, what the audience values, where a sponsor can appear, what each package includes, and how delivery and performance are measured. The reference previews are visual-language examples only. Do not copy their show, host, publisher, guests, audience metrics, testimonials, episode data, brand categories, ad formats, rates, packages, dates, or contacts.

## Canvas and grid

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `56–66 px` side margins, a `28–36 px` section header, and a `22–28 px` footer for sources or commercial validity.
- Use a 12-column grid with `16–20 px` gutters. Align positioning cards, audience metrics, demographic bars, episode rows, brand-fit categories, ad-format cards, inventory timelines, package columns, reporting notes, and contact blocks.
- Reserve `100–132 px` for section label, conclusion-first headline, and one concise explanation. Keep the lower field structured around one commercial question.
- Prefer a dark full-bleed cover, four-point positioning rows, full-width audience strips, `7/5` content-and-brand-fit splits, five-format grids, and three-package comparisons.
- Use `18–24 px` between major modules and `10–14 px` within cards. Preserve whitespace around rates and deliverables so the offer remains easy to scan.
- Most body pages should be cream and light; use near-black panels selectively for quotes, proof, premium formats, selected packages, and reporting.

## Color system

### Core palette

- Editorial cream: `#ECE2CB`. Use for the main body canvas and quiet comparison surfaces.
- Paper white: `#FFFDFC`. Use for cards, rate columns, episode rows, and clean metric fields.
- Broadcast black: `#11141A`. Use for the cover, quote panels, evidence strips, premium packages, and primary typography.
- Studio teal: `#2F8382`. Use for show identity, audience and reporting signals, selected phrases, and active navigation.
- Coral signal: `#FF6259`. Use for numbered differentiators, editorial urgency, selected values, and one contrasting commercial cue.
- Warm gray: `#827E76`. Use for secondary copy, legends, validity notes, and muted states.
- Pale rule: `#D8CEB8`. Use for dividers, chart baselines, and quiet card outlines.

### Semantic use

- Teal means owned brand identity, verified audience evidence, delivery, or measurement.
- Coral means attention, distinction, or an editorial point; it should not suggest negative performance unless explicitly labeled.
- Black panels signal authority or premium value and should not appear behind every card.
- Maintain strong contrast, especially for rates, inclusions, measurement terms, and legal notes.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `Aptos`, `Helvetica Neue`, or another confident editorial sans-serif.
- Use a restrained italic cut for one phrase in a headline, a host quote, or a short positioning line. Avoid script fonts.
- Cover title: `52–66 px`, bold. Page headline: `32–40 px`, bold. Section label: `9–11 px`, uppercase, tracked. Body: `14–17 px`. Cards and tables: `10–13 px`. Commercial terms and sources: `8–10 px`.
- Use tabular numerals for downloads, listeners, completion, geography, rates, CPM, CTR, dates, and package totals.
- Keep labels exact: downloads per episode, monthly listens, unique listeners, subscribers, completion, impressions, reach, and views are not interchangeable.

## Components

- Cards are flat white, cream, teal, or black rectangles with thin rules, small corners, and no shadow.
- Audience metric strips should show metric, value, period, aggregation method, and verification source.
- Episode rows include title, guest only when confirmed, duration, release date or episode number, and a short relevance statement.
- Brand-fit modules should identify category, audience rationale, content adjacency, and any conflict or exclusion.
- Format cards include placement, duration, host or produced voice, number of episodes, exclusivity, usage rights, channels, lead time, reporting, and price basis.
- Package columns should be directly comparable and highlight the recommended option without obscuring alternatives.

## Charts and diagrams

- Favor role or seniority bars, geography lists, listening or completion trends, episode-content rows, brand-fit matrices, ad-placement timelines, format comparisons, rate cards, package tables, and reporting cadences.
- Audience charts need period, source, platform scope, deduplication, geography, and whether values are average, median, total, or guaranteed.
- Inventory diagrams should show pre-roll, mid-roll, post-roll, newsletter, social, video, branded series, or other placements on a real episode or campaign timeline.
- Rates should identify flat fee, CPM, CPV, CPA, production fee, usage fee, minimum commitment, tax, and make-good basis as applicable.
- Reporting views should show delivery timing, data sources, attribution limitations, and third-party verification.
- Avoid 3D charts, decorative microphones as data, unsupported audience funnels, and vanity metrics without buyer relevance.

## Composition families

### On-air cover

Use a dark studio photograph or abstract audio environment, a large stacked title with teal italic emphasis, and a compact proof panel. Keep host, publisher, edition, and validity date clear.

### Show positioning

Use one sharp program statement, a short description, one verified testimonial when permitted, a host or studio portrait, and four differentiators such as guests, format, production, or owned distribution.

### Audience and reach

Use one black metric strip across the page, then split the lower field between audience role or seniority and geography or another decision-relevant dimension. Prioritize verified metrics over persona prose.

### Content and brand fit

Pair representative episode or content examples with a dark category-fit panel. Explain why the audience and editorial environment fit a category without promising brand outcomes.

### Sponsorship formats

Use a real episode anatomy or channel path above a row of format cards. Make placement, duration, recall or delivery evidence, price, and restrictions easy to compare.

### Packages, reporting, and contact

Use three package columns, select one recommended package only when appropriate, and anchor the bottom with reporting, measurement, terms, and a direct next-step contact.

## Imagery

- Use rights-cleared host portraits, studio sessions, microphones in actual context, guest conversations, waveform or transcript detail, live recordings, and owned newsletter or channel visuals.
- Keep portrait crops consistent and editorial. Show the real production environment where possible.
- Label illustrative or staged imagery. Do not imply a person is a host, guest, listener, or sponsor without permission.
- Use a minimal line-icon family for audio, newsletter, video, reporting, calendar, and contact where necessary.
- Avoid generic headphones on neon backgrounds, fake celebrity guests, anonymous stock audiences, staged handshakes, decorative sound waves, and platform logos without permission.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent downloads, listens, unique listeners, subscribers, completion, ratings, reviews, audience roles, geography, income, reach, impressions, engagement, testimonial, guest, sponsor, conversion, attribution, rate, or package outcome.
- State measurement source, platform scope, period, aggregation, invalid-traffic treatment, deduplication, and whether values are average, median, total, estimated, audited, or guaranteed.
- Distinguish downloads, streams, plays, listens, starts, views, unique users, subscribers, and newsletter readers.
- Testimonials, brand logos, guest names, episode titles, and results require permission and accurate context.
- Clearly state category exclusivity, competitive conflicts, disclosure, creative approval, cancellation, make-good, production, usage rights, and reporting terms.
- Do not promise recall, brand lift, leads, or sales without a measurement design and evidence.
- If information is missing, omit it or label it `estimate`, `target`, `illustrative`, `proposed`, `subject to availability`, or `to be confirmed`. Never invent proof to fill a rate card.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview show, host, guests, quotes, metrics, categories, ad formats, package prices, validity dates, reporting vendors, or contacts.
- Do not present cumulative downloads as average episode reach or followers as guaranteed impressions.
- Do not imply editorial endorsement, host approval, or category exclusivity without explicit terms.
- Do not use coral and teal on every border and value; preserve a stable information hierarchy.
- Do not use glossy gradients, glass cards, heavy shadows, large rounded corners, 3D charts, decorative audio visualizers, or unreadable legal copy.
- Do not hide production fees, usage rights, minimum commitments, platform limitations, or make-good conditions.
- Do not call a package best-performing without directly comparable, sourced evidence.
